title: I tried a “producer agent” style of development for a game jam, and it worked better than I expected
author: nykwil
selftext:
For the Official 2026 Unity Game Jam I wanted to try a different way of working with AI. I didn’t prompt one assistant directly. I ran several Claude Code sessions as a small team, with one acting as producer, and I stayed creative lead. The result was Hit 7, and I thought the process went quite well.

**How it was set up**

* **Small first, then Unity.** I started with a small web sim of the core loop (slot rolls, chips, cards). Bots could play it fast, so I tried rules and balance before touching the engine. For the first few days I iterated on it casually from my phone. 
* **Lanes.** Once the loop held up, I switched to Unity with only 3 days to complete. I set up one session per area, each in its own git worktree, named so they could reference each other bey name:
   * **sim**: gameplay rules and systems in Unity
   * **tune**: ran bot playthroughs and adjusted the numbers
   * **ui/audio**: menus, HUD, music and sound
   * **visuals**: effects, camera and readability
* **The producer.** It had no lane of its own. It had one measurable goal and a loop: measure, write down a prediction, get one small change built, re-measure, then log whether it was kept or reverted. It decided numbers and work order by itself. Anything that changed what the game *is* came to me. If two cycles in a row moved nothing, it had to stop and explain why.

**Why I think it worked**

* Written predictions kept it honest. Misses were on record, so it didn’t go round in circles.
* The stop rule paid off. After three failed tuning attempts, it stopped and brought me a clear design question.
* I spent my time on what only I could judge: playing builds and saying what felt wrong.
* Separating out tuning was a way to have nearly continuous validation, it could simulate heedlessly almost constantly to see how the features effected the balance.
* A page kept track of the features I requested and the status of them (and which agent was working on them)

Play it here: [https://itch.io/jam/official-unity-game-jam-2026/rate/5350957#post-17908190](https://itch.io/jam/official-unity-game-jam-2026/rate/5350957#post-17908190)

Happy to answer questions about the setup, the prompts or how the sessions talked to each other.

Rate if you have time.

comments.author: Electronic-Movie4208
comments.body: This is a really interesting approach! I esp like giving each AI its own role and using Git worktrees to avoid conflicts. Having the producer measure results and revert changes that don't work is clever. Did you run into any issues with the agents coordinating or merging their work?

replies.author: nykwil
replies.body: My lanes had very little overlap so merging was never an issue. Because velocity was key no PRs or anything. Since everything was downstream to my simulation branch gameplay development was always full steam. But that's because it was dots/ecs game so there's a clear separation of data and view inherently.

replies.author: Electronic-Movie4208
replies.body: That's a smart setup! Keeping the agents focused on separate areas clearly paid off. And using Claude Code as a whole development team is pretty impressive. Definitely one of the best AI tools out there right now!
